title: Krish Ashok Takes Food Myths From the Kitchen to the Body in 'Masala Body'
excerpt: The Masala Lab author's new book explains what the stomach, liver and intestines actually do, so readers can test the next frightening food forward themselves.
body:
• Krish Ashok, author of the bestselling Masala Lab (2021), has a new book, Masala Body: An Engineer's Guide to Eating, which applies the same first-principles science to digestion and nutrition.
  • His method: explain what the stomach, liver and intestines actually do, so readers can test frightening food claims — the kind that spread as WhatsApp forwards — for themselves.
  • Among the claims he debunks: that maida "sticks to your gut," that microwaves destroy food, and that non-stick vessels cause cancer.
  • For home cooks in the diaspora: his earlier work holds that leftover and frozen food are fine, pressure cooking does not destroy nutrients, and no food or drink "detoxes" you.

Krish Ashok made his name explaining why Indian kitchens work the way they do. In a new interview with t2ONLINE, the Chennai-based engineer and author discusses his follow-up to the bestselling Masala Lab: a second book, Masala Body: An Engineer's Guide to Eating, which takes his inquiry from the kitchen to the human body — tracing what happens to food after we eat it and separating nutritional fact from fear, misinformation and marketing.

From recipes to reasons

Ashok's starting point, in both books, is that good cooks do not think in recipes. His grandmother, he has said, thought about food as heuristics — dal was not a recipe but a pattern that could be made with any lentil, any spices, any oil. "My original interest in food science happened when I recognised that the way my grandmother or grand-aunt thought about food was fundamentally different from how recipe books tended to think about it," he told The Better India. "Cookbooks don't tell you why you need to add two cups of water for rice. They don't teach you how to adjust for more rice or how to find out if something is cooked."

"The foundational premise of the second book was that if I took a similar first-principles, layperson-friendly science approach and explained what the stomach, liver and intestines actually do, perhaps readers could work out for themselves why the next frightening WhatsApp forward didn't make sense."

— Krish Ashok, to t2ONLINE

The myth-busting method

The new book's test case is a familiar scare: the claim that maida (refined flour) sticks to your gut. As Ashok puts it, that claim is easy to debunk once you follow the digestion: eating maida spikes your blood sugar, which is a sign it is digested rapidly — "it can't both stick to your gut and also speed-run its way to your blood." The same approach runs through his earlier myth-busting: leftover food is fine and frozen food is completely fine; an air fryer or microwave is not going to give you cancer; pressure cooking does not destroy nutrients; you cannot detox by eating or drinking something; and palm oil is just another oil, to be consumed, like all oils, in moderation. "People were genuinely worried that their microwave was destroying their food or that non-stick vessels were giving them cancer," he told t2ONLINE. "These weren't abstract debates. They were concerns about what to feed their children."

Why it lands with the diaspora

Ashok, who is global head for AI Cloud Advisory and Consulting at TCS, lived abroad for seven years and learned to cook away from home — the experience that pushed him toward the science in the first place. His audience now includes exactly the cooks he once was: people in the US, Canada and the Gulf cooking Indian food with substituted ingredients, different equipment and quantities that do not match the recipe. His argument is that understanding the science is what lets you adapt — when your ingredients, equipment or quantities change, a recipe written for one kitchen stops helping, but the reasons behind it still do. As he told t2ONLINE, the aim is to show people how to examine a claim rather than dismiss it: "Otherwise, I would simply be another person on their phone asking to be believed."
